core: Working definition of LIMIT, attributed: SQLite says the SELECT returns the first N rows of its result set only; W3Schools says the SELECT TOP clause is used to limit the number of records to return

Basic shape: LIMIT N goes at the end of a SELECT query — PostgreSQL documents SELECT select_list FROM table_expression [ ORDER BY ... ] [ LIMIT { count | ALL } ]; original example SELECT * FROM products LIMIT 5;
LIMIT with ORDER BY: the classic pairing for the first N of a sorted list, e.g. the 10 most recent orders; ORDER BY mechanics owned by the sibling order-by topic, referenced only
LIMIT for pagination: OFFSET skips rows so LIMIT and OFFSET together show results in pages; PostgreSQL says OFFSET skips that many rows before beginning to return rows

Database differences: MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQLite use LIMIT; SQL Server uses TOP (Microsoft Learn documents TOP as limiting the rows returned in a query result set to a specified number of rows); Oracle uses FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY per W3Schools — the honest note, no vendor wars
LIMIT does not change the data: it is part of a SELECT, and SQLite states a SELECT statement does not make any changes to the database
Honest framing: LIMIT is small but essential — it keeps queries fast (W3Schools notes returning a large number of records can impact performance) and screens readable
supporting: PostgreSQL: if a limit count is given, no more than that many rows will be returned, but possibly fewer if the query itself yields fewer rows

PostgreSQL: when using LIMIT it is important to use an ORDER BY clause that constrains the result rows into a unique order; otherwise you get an unpredictable subset, because SQL does not promise any particular result order unless ORDER BY constrains it
SQLite: with an OFFSET clause, the first M rows are omitted from the result set and the next N rows are returned
Microsoft Learn: with ORDER BY, TOP limits the result to the first n ordered rows; otherwise TOP returns the first n rows in an undefined order
PostgreSQL: the rows skipped by an OFFSET clause still have to be computed inside the server, so a large OFFSET might be inefficient
outOfScope: Indexes and query performance tuning (own topic: indexes)

claims.claim: SQLite's SELECT reference states that with a LIMIT clause, the SELECT returns the first N rows of its result set only, where N is the value the LIMIT expression evaluates to; if the SELECT would return less than N rows without a LIMIT clause, the entire result set is returned.

PostgreSQL's documentation states that LIMIT and OFFSET allow you to retrieve just a portion of the rows that are generated by the rest of the query, and that if a limit count is given, no more than that many rows will be returned, but possibly fewer if the query itself yields fewer rows.

W3Schools states that the SELECT TOP clause is used to limit the number of records to return, that it is useful on large tables with thousands of records, and that returning a large number of records can impact performance; MySQL supports the LIMIT clause to select a limited number of records.

PostgreSQL's documentation warns that when using LIMIT it is important to use an ORDER BY clause that constrains the result rows into a unique order, because otherwise you will get an unpredictable subset of the query's rows; SQL does not promise to deliver the results of a query in any particular order unless ORDER BY is used to constrain the order.

SQLite's SELECT reference states that if a SELECT statement has an OFFSET clause, the first M rows are omitted from the result set and the next N rows are returned — the mechanism behind showing results in pages.

Microsoft Learn's TOP (Transact-SQL) reference states that TOP limits the rows returned in a query result set to a specified number of rows or percentage of rows in SQL Server, and that when TOP is used with the ORDER BY clause the result set is limited to the first n number of ordered rows; otherwise TOP returns the first n number of rows in an undefined order.
SQLite's SELECT reference states that a SELECT statement does not make any changes to the database; LIMIT is part of a SELECT query, so it caps the result without changing the data.
PostgreSQL's documentation notes that the rows skipped by an OFFSET clause still have to be computed inside the server, so a large OFFSET might be inefficient.

W3Schools shows the LIMIT-with-sort pattern: add the ORDER BY keyword when you want to sort the result, and return the first records of the sorted result; its MySQL example is SELECT * FROM Customers LIMIT 3;.

Honest framing: LIMIT is small but essential — it keeps queries fast by capping how many rows a result carries (W3Schools' performance note) and keeps screens readable through pagination, all without altering the data (SQLite's read-only property) — an interpretive framing built on the verified sources.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The clause has different names in different databases: W3Schools documents TOP as the clause used to limit the number of records to return and presents LIMIT as MySQL's equivalent, Microsoft Learn documents TOP for SQL Server, and PostgreSQL and SQLite document LIMIT.
positions: SQL Server / MS Access: SELECT TOP number ... (Microsoft Learn, W3Schools)
MySQL / PostgreSQL / SQLite: ... LIMIT number (W3Schools, PostgreSQL, SQLite)
Oracle: FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY (W3Schools)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The operation is the same — cap the result at a number of rows — and only the keyword differs by vendor. The lesson teaches LIMIT as the common form for MySQL, PostgreSQL, and SQLite, names TOP as SQL Server's equivalent with an original example, and makes no recommendation between vendors.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft described LIMIT as making the database itself faster, with no source support; the sources tie the benefit to capping a single query's result, not to the database
The draft's generic 'label on a toolbox drawer' analogy was boilerplate with no source support and was discarded
The draft's questions tested generic study skills rather than LIMIT behavior and syntax
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic draft with a definition of LIMIT attributed to SQLite (first N rows of the result set only) and W3Schools (limit the number of records to return)
Added the PostgreSQL syntax for LIMIT and OFFSET and its ORDER BY guidance (unpredictable subset without a unique order)
Added the verified database difference: LIMIT for MySQL/PostgreSQL/SQLite, TOP for SQL Server (Microsoft Learn), FETCH FIRST for Oracle (W3Schools)
Added the read-only property from SQLite (a SELECT statement does not make any changes to the database)
All SQL examples rewritten as original queries against products and orders tables, checked for standard syntax
Pagination framed simply as showing results in pages, using LIMIT with OFFSET
